header: V e r s u s.
National Bank of Pakistan and 3 others.
Present: Mirza Waqas Qayum, Advocate for petitioner.
J U D G M E N T
body: SYED MUDASSER AMEER, J. – Through this constitutional petition filed under Article 199 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973, the petitioner calls in question the failure of the respondent National Bank of Pakistan to extend to him the benefit of Promotion Policy No. 06/2016, dated 28.10.2016. He seeks promotion to the post of Senior Vice President with effect from 01.01.2017, together with all consequential benefits, on the ground that the same benefit has already been granted to other similarly placed employees pursuant to judgments of this Court, which have attained finality.

2. The petitioner joined the respondent Bank as Officer Grade-III on 01.02.1993. He was promoted to Officer Grade-II with effect from 01.01.1999, Officer Grade-I with effect from 01.12.2002, Assistant Vice President with effect from 01.01.2006, and Vice President with effect from 01.01.2012. According to him, having completed the requisite service and fulfilled the eligibility criteria, he was called for an interview for promotion to Senior Vice President on 11.09.2017 under Promotion Policy No. 06/2016. Before the promotion process could be finalized, however, the Bank introduced Promotion Policy No. 02/2017, dated 30.11.2017, and applied the revised criteria to the process already undertaken. The petitioner maintains that this deprived him of a benefit to which he was entitled under the earlier policy.

3. The controversy is not new. Several employees of the respondent Bank challenged the retrospective application of the 2017 Policy before this Court in Writ Petition No. 514-A of 2018. By judgment dated 08.11.2018, this Court allowed the petition and held that the Bank could not retrospectively apply the 2017 Policy to a promotion process already undertaken under the 2016 Policy. The Court directed the Bank to finalize the promotion cases of the petitioners in accordance with the 2016 Policy.

4. The respondent Bank challenged that judgment before the Supreme Court of Pakistan in Civil Petition No. 1761 of 2019. The petition was dismissed on 17.05.2022. The Bank's subsequent review petition, C.R.P. No. 421 of 2023, was also dismissed on 31.07.2025. The judgment dated 08.11.2018 thus attained finality. The petitioner relies upon these proceedings to contend that the legal question has already been decided and that the Bank cannot deny him the same treatment merely because he was not a party to the earlier litigation.

5. The petitioner further relies upon the judgment dated 29.10.2025 passed by this Court in Writ Petition No. 839-A of 2024, Nisar Ahmed v. National Bank of Pakistan and others. In that case, this Court set aside the Bank's speaking order dated 20.05.2024, which had declined promotion under the 2017 Policy, and directed the Bank to promote the petitioner therein to the post of Vice President with effect from the same date as his colleagues who had obtained relief under the judgment dated 08.11.2018, together with consequential benefits. The Federal Constitutional Court, by order dated 06.01.2026 in F.C.P.L.A. No. 265 of 2025, declined to interfere and refused leave to appeal.

6. The petitioner also relies upon the judgments passed by the Lahore High Court in Writ Petition No. 16996 of 2023, decided on 20.03.2024, and by the Islamabad High Court in Writ Petition No. 4396 of 2022, decided on 15.04.2026. Both judgments concerned the retrospective application of the revised promotion policy and directed that the employees' cases be dealt with under the 2016 Policy. On this basis, the petitioner asserts that the refusal to extend the same treatment to him is arbitrary, discriminatory and contrary to the law declared by the superior Courts.

7. The respondent Bank contests the petition on several grounds. It maintains that its service rules are non-statutory and that no employee has a vested right to promotion. It further asserts that promotion is a matter of policy and individual merit, and that seniority alone does not confer an enforceable right to promotion. According to the Bank, the petitioner was considered for promotion under the relevant policies but failed to meet the prescribed threshold. It is specifically contended that his score under the original version of the 2016 Policy was below the minimum required to qualify for interview and that he became eligible for consideration only after subsequent amendments. The petitioner disputes this position and claims that he fulfilled the criteria applicable to the process in which he was interviewed.

8. The principal objection, however, is that the petition is barred by laches. The Bank contends that the petitioner knew of the promotion process and the application of the revised policy in 2017, yet took no timely steps to challenge the decision. He remained silent while his colleagues pursued litigation and obtained relief. The Bank argues that he cannot now, after the success of others, seek the same benefit with retrospective effect from 01.01.2017. It is further submitted that a backdated promotion, after nearly nine years, would disturb the seniority of employees who have since been promoted and have served in higher positions. Those employees have not been impleaded, although their service interests may be affected. In the alternative, the Bank submits that, if relief is considered appropriate, any promotion should operate from the date of filing of the present petition and only if the petitioner is found eligible under the applicable policy.

9. The controversy therefore lies at the intersection of two important principles. The first is equality before the law. When a superior Court settles a question of law affecting a class of employees, the employer should ordinarily extend the same legal treatment to all who are genuinely similarly placed. The law should not become a privilege reserved for those who litigate. The second principle is that a person seeking discretionary constitutional relief must act with reasonable promptness. A litigant cannot ordinarily remain silent while a service decision is implemented, allow other employees to pursue and conclude their cases, and then seek to reopen the past when the outcome becomes favourable. This restraint becomes particularly important when the relief sought would affect the seniority and service rights of others.

10. Neither principle can be applied in isolation. Equality is not a licence to disregard delay, just as laches is not a licence for a public body to perpetuate an illegality. The task is to determine which principle governs the facts of the particular case. The answer depends upon the nature of the right asserted, the length and explanation of the delay, the degree to which the later claim is covered by the earlier judgments, and the prejudice that granting relief would cause to the respondent and to other employees. It is in this context that the petitioner's claim of parity and the Bank's objection of laches must be examined.

11. The petitioner's reliance upon Hameed Akhtar Niazi v. Secretary, Establishment Division, Government of Pakistan (1996 SCMR 1185), Government of Punjab v. Sameena Parveen (2009 SCMR 1), and Tara Chand v. Karachi Water and Sewerage Board (2005 SCMR 499) is well founded so far as the general principle of equal treatment is concerned. These authorities recognize that where the Supreme Court or a competent Tribunal decides a question of law relating to the terms and conditions of service, and the decision covers other employees who are similarly placed, the dictates of justice and good governance require that its benefit should ordinarily extend to them as well. They should not be compelled to institute separate proceedings merely to obtain the same legal determination.

12. The same principle finds support in Abdul Samad v. Federation of Pakistan (2002 SCMR 71), where the Supreme Court emphasized that similarly placed persons should not be treated differently and that the powers of the authorities must be exercised to advance, rather than thwart, the cause of justice. It also underlies the approach adopted in Ikram Bari and 524 others v. National Bank of Pakistan (2005 SCMR 100). These judgments reinforce the obligation of fairness and consistency in public administration.

13. But the rule of parity has limits. The earlier judgment must decide a question that genuinely covers the claimant, and the claimant must be similarly placed in all material respects. A common employer or a common policy does not, by itself, establish identical eligibility. Nor does a judgment in favour of one employee invariably determine the individual service entitlement of every other employee. Questions of qualification, marks, eligibility thresholds and the conditions governing a particular promotion may still require examination. Equally, the principle that the benefit of a judicial determination should extend beyond the parties does not, without more, extinguish a separate objection based upon prolonged and unexplained delay.

14. In the present case, the judgments dated 08.11.2018, 17.05.2022 and 31.07.2025 have settled the legal question that the 2017 Policy could not retrospectively deprive the employees before the Court of benefits available to them under the 2016 Policy. That declaration must be respected. It does not, however, establish that the petitioner automatically qualified for promotion to Senior Vice President or that every procedural objection to a claim raised by him years later has also been determined. The distinction between the law governing the promotion process and an individual employee's eligibility under that law must be maintained.

15. The petitioner's reliance upon Dr. Muhammad Amjad v. Dr. Israr Ahmed (2010 SCMR 1466) also requires consideration. There, the Supreme Court declined to interfere with a direction requiring the competent authority to consider an employee's promotion from the date a substantive vacancy in his promotion quota became available. The employee had become eligible in February 1997, but the Department had failed to process his case within a reasonable time. He had also pursued a representation and thereafter approached the Service Tribunal. The Court held that an employee should not suffer because of the unreasonable delay or administrative inaction of the employer.

16. That judgment establishes that a public authority cannot defeat an employee's legitimate expectation by its own unjustified delay. It does not establish that an employee may leave a known promotion grievance unchallenged for years and later seek antedated promotion without explaining his inaction. In Dr. Muhammad Amjad, the central fault lay in the Department's failure to process the employee's case in time, and the employee had pursued his grievance. In the present case, the petitioner does not allege that he was prevented from challenging the application of the 2017 Policy or pursuing an available remedy. The question is not merely whether the Bank acted lawfully in 2017, but whether discretionary relief should now be granted after prolonged inaction.

17. The petitioner next relies upon Umar Baz Khan through legal representatives v. Syed Jehanzeb and others (PLD 2013 SC 268). The Supreme Court held that laches is not a rule of universal application and cannot be applied mechanically without considering the circumstances, equity, fair play and the dictates of justice. It further observed that no Court should dismiss a case on the ground of laches where doing so would defeat justice and perpetuate an injustice. The Court also recognized that the objection requires particular care where the relief is based upon a recurring cause of action.

18. The principle is important, but it does not dispense with the need to examine the nature of the claim. Umar Baz Khan concerned the redemption of mortgaged property. The mortgagor had approached the competent authority before the expiry of the stipulated mortgage period, and the dispute thereafter continued through proceedings under a legal regime that was repealed during their pendency. The case was not one in which a litigant simply remained inactive while a completed administrative decision operated against him for years. The judgment establishes that laches must be applied according to the facts; it does not immunize every delayed claim from its operation.

19. In Jawad Khan and others v. National Database and Registration Authority (2022 PLC (C.S.) 94), this Court held that laches is relevant but not an absolute bar where employees are found entitled to relief already granted to similarly placed persons. The Court directed that the petitioners be treated like an employee who had been appointed to the posts for which they had applied and been interviewed, rather than to lower posts. The judgment was subsequently upheld by the Supreme Court in National Database and Registration Authority v. Jawad Khan and others (2023 SCMR 1381).

20. That authority gives considerable weight to the petitioner's plea of parity, but it does not conclude the present controversy. The employees in Jawad Khan had qualified the recruitment process for the advertised posts but were appointed to different and lower posts. Their claim arose from the mismatch between the advertised positions and their appointments. The present case concerns promotion under a merit-based policy, a disputed question of individual eligibility, and a claim for retrospective advancement that may alter seniority in an established service structure. The earlier judgment does not hold that a person may, without regard to these circumstances, seek antedated promotion after prolonged inaction.

21. The other authorities relied upon by the petitioner also establish that laches must be assessed in context. In Qazi Munir Ahmed v. Secretary Health (2013 PLC (C.S.) 168), the petitioner had pursued a representation against termination, and the matter had proceeded through earlier writ proceedings before the final adverse decision was challenged. In Ali Raza v. Government of Pakistan (2018 PLC (C.S.) 574), the delay was comparatively short and the controversy concerned the withdrawal of an earlier order regularizing the petitioners' services, which had conferred a vested benefit. These cases support a careful assessment of delay; neither involves the same combination of a completed promotion process, nearly nine years of inaction, and a claim to retrospective seniority.

22. In Taj Muhammad Khan v. Government of Pakistan (2020 PLC (C.S.) 668), this Court observed that the bar of laches did not apply in cases where the relief claimed was based upon a recurring cause of action. That case concerned a claim for equal pay and benefits by employees of the National Bank of Pakistan who sought the same salary package as employees performing comparable duties. The distinction is material. A continuing shortfall in recurring salary payments may give rise to a recurring financial grievance. But a decision taken in a particular promotion process is not necessarily renewed every month merely because its consequences continue to affect an employee's pay. The claim for antedated promotion, and particularly for retrospective seniority, must be examined by reference to the original decision and the subsequent service events.

23. The principle that laches is not absolute was reiterated in Benish Ghaffar v. Additional District Judge and others (2026 MLD 507). The Lahore High Court condoned a delay of more than 23 months in a family dispute where the petitioner approached the Court during the pendency of connected proceedings, relied upon subsequent developments including the birth of a minor, and the delay did not prejudice the opposite party. The Court relied, inter alia, upon FBR through Chairman, Islamabad v. Messrs Wazir Ali and Company (2020 SCMR 959) and Quetta Development Authority through Director General v. Abdul Basit and others (2022 PLC (C.S.) 288). Those decisions confirm that laches must be applied in accordance with the circumstances of each case. They do not establish that a delay approaching nine years should be overlooked when the claim may disturb the seniority of other employees who are not before the Court.

24. The principle of diligence in service matters is also illustrated by the Supreme Court's order dated 17.04.2019 in Chairman, State Life Corporation of Pakistan v. Ch. Zaheer Ahmed, Civil Petition No. 262 of 2016, which was not approved for reporting. The respondent therein sought antedated promotion to the post of Manager with effect from May 1998, although he had been promoted with effect from 18.10.2001. He first agitated the claim before the High Court in August 2006. The Supreme Court observed that the unexplained delay of about eight years in seeking antedated promotion had an adverse bearing upon inter se seniority with his colleagues. It rejected the argument that the continuing consequences of the promotion decision created a recurring cause of action. The Court also found that the respondent had failed to make out his case on the merits, converted the petition into an appeal, and set aside the High Court's order granting relief.

25. The reasoning in State Life Corporation is directly relevant. The controversy here is not confined to an isolated claim for a payment that fell due recently. The petitioner seeks retrospective promotion from 01.01.2017, with the seniority and consequential service benefits attached to that date. The underlying grievance arose when the promotion process was finalized without granting him the promotion he now claims. The fact that his pay and service prospects may continue to be affected does not, by itself, revive that original grievance indefinitely. Nor does the fact that his colleagues later succeeded in litigation necessarily erase the consequences of his own prolonged inaction.

26. The same approach is supported by Muhammad Din v. Abdul Ghani and another (2012 SCMR 1004), in which the Supreme Court held that once a constitutional petition is found to be barred by laches, the High Court is not required to decide the merits of the dispute as well. In Secretary Schools Education, Government of Punjab v. Asghari Begum and another (2023 PLC (C.S.) 214), the Supreme Court also disapproved the reopening of a service decision after a prolonged period during which the employee had failed to pursue the remedies available to her. The facts and degree of delay in that case were different, but the judgment reinforces the importance of diligence and finality in service matters.

27. The petitioner submits that the recent promotion orders issued in favour of other employees create a fresh basis for relief. The record contains orders and statements relating to the implementation of earlier judgments, including orders issued in 2024 and 2025 and statements filed in related proceedings in February 2026. Those proceedings show that the Bank has implemented judicial directions by granting promotion to the employees concerned with effect from 01.01.2017. They also explain why the petitioner now seeks the same treatment. But the implementation of judgments in favour of other litigants does not, by itself, convert the petitioner's original non-promotion into a recurring cause of action. It gives force to his claim of parity; it does not remove the need to establish that the claim is otherwise fit for discretionary relief.

28. The Bank also relies upon the recent judgment of the Federal Constitutional Court in Fazale Haq College, Mardan v. Sanobar Khan and others, decided on 20.08.2026 in connected appeals and review petitions under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The Court held, in the context of the statutory scheme governing references against land acquisition awards, that a person who had accepted an award without protest or failed to pursue the prescribed remedy could not automatically claim the benefit of enhanced compensation obtained by another landowner in separate proceedings. The Court revisited the approach in Saddaqat Ali Khan v. Collector Land Acquisition (PLD 2010 SC 878) to the extent that it had extended enhanced compensation to non-litigating owners.

29. The land acquisition judgment does not directly govern the present service dispute. The two matters arise under different legal frameworks, and the statutory period for seeking a reference under the Land Acquisition Act cannot simply be transplanted into a constitutional petition relating to promotion. Nevertheless, the judgment reinforces an important principle: a favourable decision obtained by one litigant does not invariably reopen a concluded matter for every person who did not pursue the remedy available to him. The nature of the right, the governing law, and the consequences of reopening the matter remain material. The judgment therefore supports the Bank's argument on finality, although the result here must rest upon the principles governing constitutional relief and service jurisprudence.

30. The petitioner's reliance upon the judgments in Nisar Ahmed, Writ Petition No. 16996 of 2023 and Writ Petition No. 4396 of 2022 has also been considered. Those judgments confirm that the 2017 Policy could not be used retrospectively to deprive employees, whose cases were governed by the 2016 Policy, of benefits already available to them. They strengthen the petitioner's case on the substantive question of policy. They do not, however, establish that every employee who remained inactive must receive retrospective promotion irrespective of the length of delay, individual eligibility, or prejudice to third parties. The procedural history in Nisar Ahmed was materially different. That employee pursued proceedings from 2020, sought compliance with the earlier judgment, challenged the Bank's subsequent speaking order, and obtained relief in the course of those proceedings. The Federal Constitutional Court's refusal to interfere on 06.01.2026 upheld the relief granted on that record; it did not abolish the doctrine of laches in all subsequent promotion claims.

31. The Bank's preliminary objection concerning maintainability also requires a brief answer. It relies upon Pakistan International Airlines Corporation v. Tanweer-ur-Rehman (PLD 2010 SC 676) to contend that disputes arising from non-statutory service rules fall outside constitutional jurisdiction. The objection, stated in absolute terms, is too broad. The respondent Bank is a statutory corporation, and in Muhammad Naeem v. Federation of Pakistan and others (2023 SCMR 301), the Supreme Court recognized that the Bank is amenable to the writ jurisdiction of the High Courts under Article 199, particularly in service matters governed by statutory rules. More directly, the Federal Constitutional Court in F.C.P.L.A. No. 265 of 2025 expressly treated the writ petition against NBP as competent because the Bank is a statutory body. The challenge here also concerns the allegedly unlawful retrospective application of a promotion policy that has already been examined by superior Courts. The maintainability objection, in its broad form, therefore does not furnish the basis for dismissal. That conclusion, however, does not answer the separate question of laches.

32. On the facts of this case, the delay is substantial. The petitioner knew of the disputed promotion process in 2017. The judgment dated 08.11.2018 provided a clear basis for asserting that the revised policy could not retrospectively deprive him of benefits available under the 2016 Policy. The Supreme Court upheld that judgment on 17.05.2022. Yet the petitioner did not institute the present petition until 2026. No satisfactory explanation for this prolonged inaction has been furnished. The petitioner's principal answer is that he should now receive the same benefit as his colleagues. That submission explains the claim of parity, but it does not explain why his own grievance remained unpursued while the law and service positions were being settled through earlier proceedings.

33. The consequences of the relief sought reinforce the objection. A direction for promotion with effect from 01.01.2017 would not merely result in a financial adjustment. It may alter the petitioner's inter se seniority, affect the position of employees promoted in the intervening period, and influence their prospects for further promotion. Those employees are not parties to this petition. Although the Bank has not placed a complete seniority chart identifying every person who may be affected, the potential prejudice is inherent in the nature of the relief sought. The Court should be slow to unsettle an established service structure at the instance of a person who remained inactive for years, particularly when the necessary parties have not been heard.

34. This conclusion does not mean that the earlier judgments were confined to the employees who litigated, nor that the Bank may disregard the law declared by the superior Courts. The principle in Hameed Akhtar Niazi, Sameena Parveen and Tara Chand remains important. A public employer should not compel employees to institute proceedings merely to secure equal treatment under a settled rule of law. But parity cannot be applied without examining whether the claimant is similarly placed in all material respects and whether exceptional circumstances justify overlooking his delay. The Bank has specifically disputed the petitioner's eligibility under the original version of the 2016 Policy, asserting that his score did not meet the prescribed threshold. The petitioner contests this position. That issue need not be decided here. It is enough to observe that the earlier judgments do not, by themselves, establish his individual entitlement to promotion to Senior Vice President.

35. The Bank's alternative submission that any promotion should operate from the date of filing of the petition does not alter the result. The choice of an effective date arises only after the Court finds that a claimant is entitled to relief and that the claim is not defeated by laches. A different effective date cannot, by itself, cure the prolonged inaction or remove the need to consider the rights of affected employees. In the circumstances of this case, it would not be appropriate to grant relief merely by shifting the date of promotion from 2017 to 2026.

36. The law favours equal treatment, but it does not require the Court to disregard every delay in the name of parity. The petitioner has shown that the legal question concerning retrospective application of the 2017 Policy was decided in favour of other employees. He has not, however, furnished a satisfactory explanation for waiting nearly nine years to seek the relief now claimed. The delay is substantial, the underlying grievance was known to him, and the relief sought may affect the seniority and service interests of employees who are not before the Court. The circumstances therefore bring the case within the principle applied by the Supreme Court in State Life Corporation v. Ch. Zaheer Ahmed, rather than within the exceptional cases in which laches has been overlooked to avoid a manifest injustice.

37. For the foregoing reasons, the constitutional petition is dismissed on the ground of laches. In view of this conclusion, no finding is recorded on the petitioner's individual eligibility for promotion under the 2016 Policy or on the disputed score and assessment criteria.
Announced.
J U D G E J U D G E Hon’ble Justice Abdul Fayaz & Hon’ble Justice Syed Mudasser Ameer.
